title: Two Sum
hints: Brute force is O(n^2) — try every pair. Can you trade space for time?
For each number x, you need to find target - x. What data structure gives O(1) lookup?
Walk the array once with a hash map: key = value seen, value = its index.
approach: One-pass hash map. For each nums[i], check if (target - nums[i]) is already in the map; if yes, return both indices. Otherwise store nums[i] -> i.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
hints: You only do one buy and one sell. The buy must come before the sell.
Track the cheapest price seen so far as you scan left to right.
At each day, the best profit ending today is price[today] - min_so_far.
approach: Single pass tracking min price seen and max profit. Update min if today is lower; otherwise update max profit with today - min.

title: Contains Duplicate
hints: Sorting makes duplicates adjacent — but costs O(n log n).
A set gives O(1) membership checks.
Compare len(set(nums)) to len(nums) for a one-liner.
approach: Insert into a set as you scan; return True the moment you see a repeat. Or compare set size to list size.

title: Product of Array Except Self
hints: No division allowed. Think about prefix and suffix products.
answer[i] = (product of everything left of i) * (product of everything right of i).
Do it in two passes: left products into the output, then multiply by running right product.
approach: Two passes. First pass fills answer[i] with prefix product. Second pass walks right-to-left, multiplying answer[i] by the running suffix product.
solution:
def productExceptSelf(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = left
        left *= nums[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= right
        right *= nums[i]
    return out

title: Maximum Subarray
hints: Classic Kadane's algorithm.
At each index, either extend the previous subarray or start fresh from here.
cur = max(nums[i], cur + nums[i]); best = max(best, cur).
approach: Kadane: maintain the best sum ending at i. Reset to nums[i] when running sum goes negative.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
hints: Negatives flip max into min and vice versa, so track both.
Maintain max_ending_here and min_ending_here at each index.
On a negative, swap them before extending.
approach: Track running max and min. At each step: candidates are x, x*cur_max, x*cur_min. The min matters because two negatives become a big positive.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
hints: O(log n) suggests binary search.
Compare nums[mid] to nums[right] to decide which half holds the minimum.
If nums[mid] > nums[right], the min is in the right half; otherwise it is in the left half (including mid).
approach: Binary search on the rotation pivot. Use nums[right] as the anchor — it lies in the lower section after rotation.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
hints: Binary search, but you must decide which half is sorted at each step.
Compare nums[lo] to nums[mid]: if nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted.
Check whether target falls inside the sorted half; if yes, search there, else the other half.
approach: Modified binary search. One half is always sorted — locate it, check if target is in that range, recurse accordingly.

title: Sum of Two Integers
hints: XOR gives sum without carry. AND-then-shift gives the carry.
Loop: sum = a XOR b, carry = (a AND b) << 1, then repeat until carry is 0.
Python has unbounded ints, so mask to 32 bits and re-interpret negatives via two's complement.
approach: Bit-manipulation full adder. Mask with 0xFFFFFFFF to simulate 32-bit overflow, then convert back to signed at the end.

title: Number of 1 Bits
hints: Loop n and look at the last bit with n & 1, then n >>= 1.
Faster trick: n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit — iterate until n is 0.
Python builtin: bin(n).count('1').
approach: Brian Kernighan's algorithm: each pass n &= n - 1 strips exactly one set bit, so loop count == number of set bits.

complexity.time: O(k) where k is the number of set bits

title: Counting Bits
hints: Naive: call popcount on each i — O(n log n).
Use DP: bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1).
Alternative: bits[i] = bits[i & (i - 1)] + 1.
approach: Dynamic programming on previously computed values. bits[i] = bits[i//2] + (i mod 2): drop the last bit, add it back if it was 1.

title: Missing Number
hints: Sum trick: expected sum is n*(n+1)/2 — subtract the actual sum.
XOR trick: XOR all indices 0..n and all values; pairs cancel, the missing number remains.
Both run in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.
approach: XOR all indices [0..n] with all array values. Equal values cancel out; the leftover is the missing number.

title: Reverse Bits
hints: Loop 32 times: pull the bottom bit off n, push it onto result.
result = (result << 1) | (n & 1); n >>= 1.
For repeated calls, you can cache reversals of 8-bit chunks.
approach: Shift result left and OR in the lowest bit of n, 32 times.

title: Climbing Stairs
hints: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2): last step is either 1 or 2.
This is the Fibonacci sequence — keep only two prior values.
Base cases: ways(1) = 1, ways(2) = 2.
approach: Fibonacci recurrence with two rolling variables.

title: Coin Change
hints: Unbounded knapsack. dp[i] = fewest coins to make amount i.
Transition: dp[i] = min(dp[i - c] + 1) over each coin c <= i.
Initialize dp[0] = 0, others to infinity; return dp[amount] (or -1 if still infinity).
approach: Bottom-up DP over amounts. For each amount, try each coin and take the min.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
hints: O(n^2) DP: dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) for j < i with nums[j] < nums[i].
For O(n log n), maintain a 'tails' array — smallest tail value for each LIS length.
Use bisect_left to find where the current number belongs in 'tails'.
approach: Patience sorting with binary search. tails[k] = smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
hints: Classic 2D DP on (i, j) = prefix lengths of text1 and text2.
If text1[i-1] == text2[j-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; else max of dropping one char from either side.
You can compress to two rows since each row only depends on the previous.
approach: 2D DP. Fill an (m+1) x (n+1) table; answer is dp[m][n].

title: Word Break
hints: dp[i] = True iff s[:i] can be segmented.
Transition: dp[i] is True if some j < i has dp[j] True and s[j:i] in dict.
Use a set for O(1) dictionary lookups.
approach: 1D DP over prefixes. For each position, check every earlier breakpoint.

title: Combination Sum IV
hints: Order matters here — (1,2) and (2,1) are different. So iterate target on the outside.
dp[t] = sum over n in nums of dp[t - n] when n <= t.
Base: dp[0] = 1 (one way to make 0: take nothing).
approach: 1D DP. Outer loop over target, inner loop over nums — that ordering counts permutations.

title: House Robber
hints: At each house, either rob it (and skip the previous) or skip it.
dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]).
Only the last two values matter — keep two variables.
approach: Linear DP with two rolling variables prev (i-2) and cur (i-1).

title: House Robber II
hints: Circular constraint: you cannot pick both house 0 and house n-1.
Split into two linear House Robber subproblems: nums[0:n-1] and nums[1:n].
Return the larger of the two.
approach: Run House Robber I twice, each time excluding one endpoint of the circle.

title: Decode Ways
hints: At each position, you either decode a single digit (1-9) or a pair (10-26).
Beware leading zeros: '0' alone has no decoding, and '06' is not valid.
approach: 1D DP. At each index, add ways from the previous index when the single digit is valid, and from two-back when the two-digit code is valid.

title: Unique Paths
hints: Paths to (i, j) = paths to (i-1, j) + paths to (i, j-1).
Closed form: C(m+n-2, m-1) — count of ways to arrange (m-1) downs among (m+n-2) moves.
DP with one row suffices.
approach: Combinatorial formula or 1D DP that overwrites a row left-to-right.

title: Jump Game
hints: Greedy: track the farthest index reachable so far.
Scan left to right; if i exceeds reach, you're stuck.
Stop early when reach >= last index.
approach: Single-pass greedy. Maintain max reachable index; fail if you ever stand beyond it.

title: Clone Graph
hints: DFS or BFS, but you must remember mappings so cycles don't loop forever.
Map original-node -> cloned-node in a dict.
When visiting a neighbor, look it up; create it only if absent.
approach: DFS with a hash map from original to clone. Recurse on each neighbor, populating clone.neighbors as you go.

title: Course Schedule
hints: This is cycle detection in a directed graph.
Either run Kahn's algorithm (BFS over in-degree 0 nodes) or DFS with a visiting/visited color set.
If you process every course (Kahn) or never revisit a node in the current path (DFS), it's possible.
approach: Kahn's topological sort. Build adjacency list and in-degrees; repeatedly take a node with in-degree 0 and decrement its neighbors' in-degrees. Finishable iff you process all courses.
solution:
from collections import deque, defaultdict

def canFinish(numCourses, prerequisites):
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    indeg = [0] * numCourses
    for a, b in prerequisites:
        graph[b].append(a)
        indeg[a] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(numCourses) if indeg[i] == 0)
    done = 0
    while q:
        c = q.popleft()
        done += 1
        for nxt in graph[c]:
            indeg[nxt] -= 1
            if indeg[nxt] == 0:
                q.append(nxt)
    return done == numCourses

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
hints: Reverse the flow: start from each ocean's border and walk uphill (or equal).
Two DFS/BFS passes — one from Pacific edges, one from Atlantic edges.
The answer is the intersection of cells reached by both.
approach: Multi-source DFS from each ocean's border, moving only to cells with equal or greater height. Cells in both visited sets are the answer.

title: Number of Islands
hints: Scan the grid; each unvisited '1' starts a new island.
From each starting cell, flood-fill (DFS or BFS) all connected '1's, marking them visited.
Either mutate the grid (set to '0') or use a visited set.
approach: Iterate cells; when a '1' is found, increment count and DFS to sink the whole island.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
hints: Sorting works in O(n log n); the O(n) trick uses a set.
Put everything in a set; for each x, only start counting if x-1 is NOT in the set (so x is a sequence start).
Then walk x+1, x+2, ... while present.
approach: Hash set of all values. For each potential sequence start (no predecessor in set), expand forward and track max length.

title: Alien Dictionary
hints: Compare each pair of adjacent words — the first differing char gives one ordering edge.
Build a directed graph of letters, then topological sort it.
Watch the edge case: if word A is longer than word B and A is a prefix of B, the input is invalid (return '').
approach: Extract ordering edges from adjacent-word pairs, run Kahn's BFS for topological order. Failure cases: cycle detected, or invalid prefix.

title: Graph Valid Tree
hints: A tree on n nodes has exactly n-1 edges AND is connected AND has no cycle.
If edges == n-1 and the graph is connected, it must be acyclic.
Use Union-Find: if a union ever joins two nodes already in the same set, there's a cycle.
approach: Union-Find with path compression. Reject if a union sees two nodes with the same root, otherwise verify edges == n-1.

title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
hints: Start with n components; each edge that joins two previously separate components reduces the count by 1.
Union-Find naturally tracks this.
Alternative: build adjacency list, then DFS/BFS counting components.
approach: Union-Find. Initialize count = n; each successful union (different roots) decrements it.

title: Insert Interval
hints: Three phases: intervals strictly left, overlapping ones to merge, intervals strictly right.
While the current interval ends before newInterval starts, copy it through.
While intervals overlap with newInterval, expand newInterval; then copy the rest.
approach: Three-phase scan: append non-overlapping lefts, merge overlapping ones into newInterval, append the rest.
solution:
def insert(intervals, newInterval):
    res = []
    i, n = 0, len(intervals)
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < newInterval[0]:
        res.append(intervals[i]); i += 1
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= newInterval[1]:
        newInterval[0] = min(newInterval[0], intervals[i][0])
        newInterval[1] = max(newInterval[1], intervals[i][1])
        i += 1
    res.append(newInterval)
    res.extend(intervals[i:])
    return res

title: Merge Intervals
hints: Sort by start time first.
Walk through; if the current interval overlaps the last result, extend the last's end.
Otherwise append the current interval.
approach: Sort by start, then sweep. Merge when current.start <= last.end.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
hints: Classic greedy: sort by end time.
Always keep the interval that finishes earliest among those that don't conflict.
Count and remove the rest.
approach: Sort by end. Greedily accept any interval whose start >= last kept end. Removed count = total - kept.

title: Meeting Rooms
hints: Sort by start time.
If any meeting starts before the previous one ends, return False.
Otherwise True.
approach: Sort by start; verify each meeting begins no earlier than the previous one ends.

title: Meeting Rooms II
hints: Min-heap of end times: at any moment its size is the number of rooms in use.
Sort intervals by start. For each meeting, pop ended rooms before pushing this meeting's end.
Final heap size is the answer.
approach: Sort by start, then sweep with a min-heap of end times. Reuse rooms whose end <= current start.

title: Reverse Linked List
hints: Iterative: walk with prev = None, cur = head; flip cur.next, advance.
Save next before clobbering cur.next or you lose the rest of the list.
Recursive variation: reverse the tail, then point head.next.next = head.
approach: Iterative three-pointer flip.
solution:
def reverseList(head):
    prev = None
    cur = head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = nxt
    return prev

title: Linked List Cycle
hints: Floyd's tortoise and hare: two pointers, slow steps 1, fast steps 2.
If they meet, there's a cycle. If fast hits None, there isn't.
Alternative: use a visited set — but that's O(n) space.
approach: Two-pointer (Floyd) cycle detection.

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
hints: Use a dummy head node so you don't special-case the first append.
Walk both lists, attaching whichever current node is smaller.
When one is exhausted, attach the rest of the other.
approach: Dummy-head iterative merge.

title: Merge K Sorted Lists
hints: Naive: concatenate all and sort — O(N log N).
Better: min-heap of size k holding the front of each list. Pop the smallest, push its next.
Alternative: pairwise merge using divide-and-conquer.
approach: Min-heap of (value, list_index, node). Pop smallest, advance, push its successor.

title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
hints: Two-pointer with a gap of n.
Move 'fast' n steps ahead first; then move both until fast hits the end. Slow is now at the node before the one to remove.
Use a dummy head to simplify removing the head itself.
approach: Two pointers separated by n, advanced together until the leading one reaches the end.

title: Reorder List
hints: Three subproblems: find middle, reverse second half, interleave the two halves.
Use slow/fast pointers to find the middle.
Carefully terminate the first half before reversing the second.
approach: Split with slow/fast, reverse second half in place, then weave nodes together.
solution:
def reorderList(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return
    slow = fast = head
    while fast.next and fast.next.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    prev, cur = None, slow.next
    slow.next = None
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = nxt
    first, second = head, prev
    while second:
        t1, t2 = first.next, second.next
        first.next = second
        second.next = t1
        first, second = t1, t2

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
hints: Naive uses O(m+n) extra space to mark rows and columns.
O(1) trick: use the first row and first column themselves as markers.
Handle the first row/column separately with two boolean flags.
approach: Use row 0 and column 0 as scratch space for zero flags; track the original state of those two with two booleans.

title: Spiral Matrix
hints: Track four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right.
Walk right across top row, down the right column, left across bottom row, up the left column. Shrink boundaries after each side.
Check that top <= bottom and left <= right before each pass to avoid double-counting.
approach: Layer-by-layer with four boundaries.

title: Rotate Image
hints: 90 clockwise = transpose + reverse each row.
Transpose: swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for i < j.
Then reverse each row in place.
approach: Transpose in place, then reverse each row.

title: Word Search
hints: Backtracking DFS from every cell that matches word[0].
Mark visited cells temporarily (e.g., overwrite with '#'), restore on backtrack.
Prune as soon as a mismatch occurs or you walk off-grid.
approach: DFS with in-place marking. Try all four neighbors; restore cell after returning.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
hints: Sliding window with two pointers.
Use a dict mapping char -> last seen index.
When you see a duplicate, jump left to max(left, last_seen[char] + 1).
approach: Sliding window; left pointer jumps past the last occurrence of any repeated character.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
hints: Sliding window with a frequency map.
Window is valid iff (window_length - count_of_most_frequent_char) <= k.
If invalid, shrink from the left.
approach: Sliding window. Maintain max frequency in the window; window must satisfy size - maxFreq <= k.
solution:
from collections import defaultdict

def characterReplacement(s, k):
    counts = defaultdict(int)
    left = best = max_count = 0
    for right, c in enumerate(s):
        counts[c] += 1
        max_count = max(max_count, counts[c])
        while (right - left + 1) - max_count > k:
            counts[s[left]] -= 1
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

title: Minimum Window Substring
hints: Sliding window with a 'have/need' counter.
Expand right until window contains all of t's chars; then shrink left while still valid.
Track the best (shortest) valid window seen.
approach: Sliding window with character counts. Track how many distinct chars currently meet their target count.

title: Valid Anagram
hints: Two anagrams have the same character counts.
Sort both and compare — O(n log n).
Or count chars in one pass with Counter / array of 26 ints — O(n).
approach: Compare character frequency counts.

title: Group Anagrams
hints: Anagrams share a canonical form — either sorted string or a 26-tuple of counts.
Use that as a dict key and append each word to its bucket.
Tuple of counts is O(n) per word; sorted string is O(n log n).
approach: Hash words by their character-count signature.

title: Valid Parentheses
hints: Use a stack.
Push opens; when you see a close, the stack top must match.
At the end the stack should be empty.
approach: Stack of opening brackets; match on close, fail on mismatch or empty stack.

title: Valid Palindrome
hints: Two-pointer from both ends.
Skip non-alphanumeric chars; lowercase before comparing.
Return False on first mismatch.
approach: Two pointers converging, skipping non-alphanumerics.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
hints: Expand around each possible center: 2n-1 centers (between each char and at each char).
For each center, expand outward while both sides match.
Track the longest seen. Manacher's gives O(n) but is overkill for 1000.
approach: Expand around centers, both odd-length and even-length.

title: Palindromic Substrings
hints: Same expand-around-center trick.
Each successful expansion contributes one palindromic substring.
Sum across all centers.
approach: Expand around each center, counting palindromes formed.

title: Encode and Decode Strings
hints: Use a length-prefixed encoding so any character (including delimiters) can appear in the strings.
Format each as '<len>#<string>'.
Decode by reading until '#', parsing the length, then slicing that many chars.
approach: Length-prefix each string with a delimiter separator.

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
hints: Recursion: depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)).
Base case: null node has depth 0.
BFS works too — count levels.
approach: Recursive max of children plus one.

title: Same Tree
hints: Structural recursion: both null = same; one null = different.
Otherwise values must match AND left/right subtrees must each be same.
Short-circuit on first mismatch.
approach: Recurse comparing values and corresponding subtrees.

title: Invert Binary Tree
hints: At each node, swap left and right.
Recurse into both subtrees (order doesn't matter).
Iterative variant: BFS/DFS with an explicit stack/queue.
approach: Recursive swap.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
hints: At each node, the path 'through' the node = node.val + max(0, left_gain) + max(0, right_gain).
But the value RETURNED upward can only extend into one child: node.val + max(0, max(left_gain, right_gain)).
Track the global best inside the recursion.
approach: DFS returning the best one-sided gain; meanwhile update a global best with the through-node sum.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
hints: BFS with a queue, processing one level at a time.
At each step, snapshot the current queue size — that's the level width.
Pop exactly that many nodes per level into a sublist.
approach: BFS in level-sized batches.

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
hints: Pick a consistent traversal (preorder is easy) and mark null children explicitly.
Serialize: preorder DFS, emit 'null' for absent children, comma-separate.
Deserialize: split tokens, build via the same preorder using an iterator.
approach: Preorder with explicit null markers.

title: Subtree of Another Tree
hints: Walk every node of root; from each, check 'same tree' against subRoot.
'Same tree' is the helper from problem 100.
Faster: serialize both trees and check substring (with care for null markers).
approach: DFS over root; at each node test sameTree(node, subRoot).

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
hints: First element of preorder is the root.
Find its position in inorder — left side is the left subtree, right side is the right subtree.
Use an index map for O(1) inorder lookup.
approach: Recursive split using a hash map for inorder positions.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
hints: Each node must lie within an allowed (low, high) range that tightens as you descend.
Going left: high becomes node.val. Going right: low becomes node.val.
Alternative: inorder traversal must be strictly increasing.
approach: Recursive range validation.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
hints: BST inorder traversal visits nodes in sorted order.
Stop at the kth visited node.
Iterative inorder with an explicit stack lets you stop early without traversing the whole tree.
approach: Iterative inorder; stop when the visit count reaches k.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
hints: Use BST ordering to navigate.
If both p and q are less than node, go left; if both greater, go right.
Otherwise the current node splits them — that's the LCA.
approach: Walk down the BST until p and q diverge.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
hints: Count frequencies with a hash map.
Bucket sort by frequency — n+1 buckets indexed by count — gives O(n).
Min-heap of size k is a clean alternative: O(n log k).
approach: Bucket sort by frequency: index i holds values that appear exactly i times.

title: Find Median from Data Stream
hints: Two heaps: max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper half.
Keep them balanced (sizes differ by at most 1).
Median = top of the larger heap, or average of both tops when equal.
approach: Two heaps with rebalancing after every insert.

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
hints: Sorting is O(n log n) — fine but not optimal.
Min-heap of size k: O(n log k).
Quickselect: average O(n), worst O(n^2).
approach: Min-heap of size k; top is the kth largest.

title: 3Sum
hints: Sort the array first — that's what makes dedup tractable.
For each i, do a two-pointer search on the suffix for pairs summing to -nums[i].
Skip duplicate values for i, left, and right to avoid duplicate triplets.
approach: Sort, then for each pivot run two-pointer on the right side. Skip duplicates carefully.

title: Container With Most Water
hints: Two pointers at both ends.
Area = min(left_height, right_height) * (right - left).
Always move the shorter side inward — the only way to potentially find a taller bound.
approach: Two pointers converging; advance whichever side is shorter.

title: Trapping Rain Water
hints: Water above index i is min(maxLeft[i], maxRight[i]) - height[i].
Precompute both arrays for an O(n) time / O(n) space solution.
Two-pointer trick removes the extra arrays for O(1) space.
approach: Two pointers tracking max so far from each side. Move from the shorter side and accumulate trapped water.
solution:
def trap(height):
    l, r = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max = right_max = 0
    water = 0
    while l < r:
        if height[l] < height[r]:
            left_max = max(left_max, height[l])
            water += left_max - height[l]
            l += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, height[r])
            water += right_max - height[r]
            r -= 1
    return water

title: Move Zeroes
hints: Two pointers: a slow 'write' index for non-zero elements.
Scan with a fast pointer; whenever you see non-zero, copy to write and advance write.
Fill the rest with zeros, or swap as you go to avoid a second pass.
approach: Two-pointer in-place: swap non-zero elements forward.
